Credit Risk Analysis: who is likely to miss next month's payment?¶

The question: a Taiwanese bank recorded 30,000 credit-card customers in 2005: their credit limit, a few demographic facts, six months of repayment status, bill amounts and payment amounts. Did each customer default the following month? Which facts predict default, how well can a model rank customers by risk, can we trust its probabilities, and is the model fair to different groups of customers?

How this notebook works. Each section starts with a plain-English explanation, then the code, then a "how to read this" note.

  1. The analogy
  2. Setup
  3. Audit the data
  4. Hypotheses and why we chose each test
  5. H1: does payment history predict default?
  6. H2: does the credit limit matter?
  7. H3: demographics, and the odds ratios when everything is held fixed
  8. H4: overlapping bill columns
  9. H5: a leak-free model ladder (and do we need the demographics?)
  10. H6: can we trust the probabilities?
  11. H7: deciding who to decline, and is it fair?
  12. Takeaways
  13. Limitations

Run it: uv run jupyter lab ML/credit-risk-analysis/credit_risk_analysis.ipynb, or Run All in any Jupyter. The data downloads itself from the UCI repository on the first run (about 5 MB).

1. 💡 The simple analogy¶

Think of a teacher trying to guess which students will hand in next week's homework late. Who would they bet on?

  • A student who has been late for the last three weeks is the obvious worry. Recent behaviour is the strongest clue.
  • A student whose homework pile is huge compared with their time (a big load relative to their limit) is also at risk.
  • The student's age, family or gender shouldn't matter, and if a teacher did bet on them, we would call that unfair. A good predictor shouldn't need them.

Credit risk is the same game with money: payment history first, load second, and personal characteristics should add (almost) nothing. The twist is that a bank's guesses affect real people, so besides accuracy we will check honesty (are the predicted probabilities right?) and fairness (does the model treat groups similarly?).

2. Setup¶

What: imports and named constants. Why: one place for numbers like the random seed keeps the notebook reproducible and avoids "magic numbers". With the seed fixed, every bootstrap and cross-validation split comes out the same each time you run it.

def fmt_p(p: float) -> str:
    """Formats a p-value, showing values below floating-point precision honestly.

    Args:
        p: The p-value.

    Returns:
        A short string such as ``3.2e-08`` or ``< 1e-300``.
    """
    return "< 1e-300" if p < 1e-300 else f"{p:.1e}"

3. Audit the data first¶

What: load the file and check what each column means. Why: the columns of this dataset are encoded in ways that are easy to misread.

  • PAY_0, PAY_2 ... PAY_6: repayment status for September back to April 2005 (the first column is called PAY_0, not PAY_1, and there is no PAY_1). The codes are: −2 = no consumption (no balance to pay), −1 = paid in full, 0 = paid only the minimum on a revolving balance, 1, 2, 3 ... = payment delayed by that many months. So the column mixes "good" codes (−2, −1, 0) with a count of months late, and it is not a plain number.
  • BILL_AMT1..6 are the statement amounts and PAY_AMT1..6 the amounts actually paid, both in New Taiwan dollars.
  • LIMIT_BAL is the credit limit, and SEX (1 male, 2 female), EDUCATION (1 graduate school, 2 university, 3 high school, 4 other), MARRIAGE (1 married, 2 single, 3 other) and AGE are demographics.
  • The documentation only defines EDUCATION codes 1 to 4 and MARRIAGE codes 1 to 3, yet the file also contains EDUCATION 0, 5 and 6 and MARRIAGE 0. We fold the undocumented codes into "other" and say so, instead of hiding it. (The legacy script did this too, with a comment admitting it "incorrectly" maps them.)
In [2]:
def load_credit_default(path: Path = DATA_PATH) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Loads the UCI "Default of Credit Card Clients" data, downloading it on first use.

    Args:
        path: Where to cache the Excel file extracted from the UCI zip archive.

    Returns:
        DataFrame with 23 features and a binary ``default`` target (30,000 rows).

    Raises:
        ValueError: If the sheet does not have the expected shape or contains nulls.
    """
    if not path.exists():
        path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
        with urllib.request.urlopen(DATA_URL) as response:  # noqa: S310 - fixed https URL
            archive = zipfile.ZipFile(io.BytesIO(response.read()))
        path.write_bytes(archive.read(archive.namelist()[0]))
    table = pd.read_excel(path, header=1).drop(columns="ID")
    table = table.rename(columns={"default payment next month": "default"})
    if table.shape != (30_000, 24) or table.isna().any().any():
        raise ValueError(f"Unexpected data: shape={table.shape}")
    return table

    f"Undocumented codes: EDUCATION in (0, 5, 6): {int(raw['EDUCATION'].isin([0, 5, 6]).sum())} "
    f"customers; MARRIAGE = 0: {int((raw['MARRIAGE'] == 0).sum())} customers"
)

data = raw.drop_duplicates().reset_index(drop=True)
data["EDUCATION"] = data["EDUCATION"].replace({0: 4, 5: 4, 6: 4})
data["MARRIAGE"] = data["MARRIAGE"].replace({0: 3})

X = data.drop(columns="default")

print(

    f"(catches 0 of {int(y.sum()):,} defaults)"
)

How to read this. There are 30,000 customers with no missing values, and 35 exact duplicate rows, which we remove so that a twin can't sit on both sides of a cross-validation split. About 22.1% of customers default the next month, so "approve everyone" would be right about 77.9% of the time while catching no defaults: accuracy isn't a useful scoreboard here, so we'll use ROC-AUC (the chance the model scores a random defaulter above a random non-defaulter), average precision and calibration.

The credit limits range widely (the table shows a median of about 140,000 NT dollars but a maximum of 1,000,000), and some bill amounts are negative (a customer who overpaid has a credit balance).

4. 🔬 Hypotheses and why we chose each test¶

Here are the questions, each with its null (H₀, "nothing special") and alternative (Hₐ), written before looking at any p-values:

# Question H₀ Hₐ Method
H1 Does last month's repayment status relate to default? Default rate is the same for every status It differs Chi-square test, Cramér's V, Wilson CIs
H2 Do defaulters have different credit limits? Same distribution Different Mann-Whitney U with Cliff's δ
H3 Do demographics relate to default, and do they still matter once payment behaviour is held fixed? Odds ratio = 1 OR ≠ 1 Chi-square with Cramér's V; adjusted logistic regression odds ratios
H4 Are the six bill columns independent pieces of information? (descriptive) They overlap heavily Correlations and variance inflation factors (VIF)
H5 Do complex models beat logistic regression, and do we need SEX, AGE and MARRIAGE? AUC difference = 0 A difference exists Leak-free repeated stratified CV with paired Nadeau-Bengio tests
H6 Are the predicted probabilities honest? Predicted = observed default rate in every risk band They differ Calibration curve, Brier score, Hosmer-Lemeshow test
H7 Does the model treat groups similarly? Same false-positive rate in both groups Rates differ Two-proportion z-test on out-of-fold decisions

Why chi-square and Cramér's V? The chi-square test compares the observed counts in a table (status × default) with what we'd see if status and default were unrelated. With 30,000 customers it will flag anything, so we always report Cramér's V (0 = no association, 1 = perfect) as the effect size. Why Mann-Whitney U and Cliff's δ? Mann-Whitney U lines everyone up and asks whether one group tends to sit higher. Cliff's δ is P(group A higher) − P(group A lower) from −1 to +1 (|δ| about 0.15 small, 0.33 medium, 0.47 large). Why an odds ratio? The odds of default are chance of default ÷ chance of not defaulting, and the odds ratio (OR) compares two groups' odds (1 = no difference, 2 = double the odds).

5. H1: does payment history predict default?¶

What: the default rate for each value of last month's repayment status PAY_0, with Wilson 95% intervals (a well-behaved CI for proportions), plus a chi-square test of H₀: the default rate is the same for every status.

status = data["PAY_0"]
by_status = pd.DataFrame(
    {"customers": status.value_counts().sort_index(), "defaults": y.groupby(status).sum()}
)
by_status["rate"] = by_status["defaults"] / by_status["customers"]
by_status["ci_low"], by_status["ci_high"] = proportion_confint(
    by_status["defaults"], by_status["customers"], method="wilson"
)

table = pd.crosstab(status, y)
chi2, p_status, dof, _ = stats.chi2_contingency(table)
cramers_v = np.sqrt(chi2 / table.to_numpy().sum() / (min(table.shape) - 1))
print(f"Chi-square: chi2({dof}) = {chi2:.0f}, p = {fmt_p(p_status)}, Cramer's V = {cramers_v:.2f}")

How to read this. The chi-square test gives χ²(10) ≈ 5,300 and p ≈ 0, with Cramér's V ≈ 0.42, a large effect, so we reject H₀. In the chart, the three teal bars are customers who are not late (no use, paid in full, minimum only) and default at about 13% to 17%. The orange bars are customers who were late last month: one month late is a 34% default rate, and two months late about 69%. Beyond three months the groups are tiny (a few dozen customers or fewer), so their error bars are wide: the direction is clear (more than 50%), the exact percentages are not.

This is the "late homework" rule from the analogy, confirmed: recent payment behaviour is by far the strongest clue.

6. H2: does the credit limit matter?¶

What: compare the credit limit of customers who defaulted with those who didn't. Why Mann-Whitney U? Limits are very right-skewed (a few customers have enormous limits), so a rank-based test is safer than comparing averages.

In [5]:
limit_default = data.loc[y == 1, "LIMIT_BAL"]
limit_ok = data.loc[y == 0, "LIMIT_BAL"]
mwu_limit = stats.mannwhitneyu(limit_default, limit_ok)
delta_limit = 2 * mwu_limit.statistic / (len(limit_default) * len(limit_ok)) - 1
decile = pd.qcut(data["LIMIT_BAL"], 10, duplicates="drop")
rate_by_limit = y.groupby(decile, observed=True).mean()

print(
    f"Median credit limit: defaulters {limit_default.median():,.0f}, "
    f"others {limit_ok.median():,.0f}"
)
print(f"Mann-Whitney p = {fmt_p(mwu_limit.pvalue)}, Cliff's delta = {delta_limit:+.2f}")
print(
    f"Default rate in the lowest-limit decile {rate_by_limit.iloc[0]:.1%} vs highest "
    f"{rate_by_limit.iloc[-1]:.1%}"
)

Mann-Whitney p = 6.1e-190, Cliff's delta = -0.24
Default rate in the lowest-limit decile 35.8% vs highest 11.8%

How to read this. Defaulters have a lower median limit (90,000 against 150,000 NT dollars), with Cliff's δ ≈ −0.24 (a small-to-medium effect) and p ≈ 1e-189, so we reject H₀. The decile chart shows a steady downward staircase: the lowest-limit tenth of customers default at roughly three times the rate of the highest-limit tenth. A plausible reading: banks give bigger limits to customers who already look safe, so the limit partly echoes the bank's own earlier judgement.

7. H3: demographics, and the odds ratios when everything is held fixed¶

What: first, how big is the raw link between each demographic and default? We show the default rate per group, with Cramér's V from a chi-square test. Then we ask the sharper question: once payment behaviour is held fixed, do demographics still matter? For that we fit a logistic regression (with statsmodels, which gives odds ratios with confidence intervals) using a few plain-English summaries of behaviour plus the demographics. H₀: the odds ratio for a feature is 1.

In [6]:
def age_band(age: pd.Series) -> pd.Series:
    """Buckets ages into four readable bands.

    Args:
        age: Ages in years.

    Returns:
        Categorical band labels.
    """
    return pd.cut(age, [0, 29, 39, 49, 100], labels=["under 30", "30s", "40s", "50+"])


groups = {
    "SEX": data["SEX"].map({1: "male", 2: "female"}),
    "EDUCATION": data["EDUCATION"].map(
        {1: "graduate", 2: "university", 3: "high school", 4: "other"}
    ),
    "MARRIAGE": data["MARRIAGE"].map({1: "married", 2: "single", 3: "other"}),
    "AGE": age_band(data["AGE"]),
}
raw_effects = {}
for name, labels_series in groups.items():
    crosstab = pd.crosstab(labels_series, y)
    chi2_g, p_g, _, _ = stats.chi2_contingency(crosstab)
    v = np.sqrt(chi2_g / crosstab.to_numpy().sum() / (min(crosstab.shape) - 1))
    raw_effects[name] = {
        "chi2": chi2_g,
        "p": p_g,
        "cramers_v": v,
        "highest default rate": y.groupby(labels_series, observed=True).mean().max(),
        "lowest default rate": y.groupby(labels_series, observed=True).mean().min(),
    }
raw_effects = pd.DataFrame(raw_effects).T
raw_effects["p_holm"] = multipletests(raw_effects["p"].astype(float), method="holm")[1]
raw_effects.style.format(
    {
        "chi2": "{:.0f}",
        "p": fmt_p,
        "cramers_v": "{:.3f}",
        "highest default rate": "{:.1%}",
        "lowest default rate": "{:.1%}",
        "p_holm": fmt_p,
    }
)

def behaviour_summary(frame: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Plain-English summaries of payment behaviour.

    Args:
        frame: Customer table with PAY_*, BILL_AMT*, PAY_AMT* and LIMIT_BAL columns.

    Returns:
        DataFrame with the worst delay (months), number of late months, average credit
        utilisation (average bill divided by the limit) and the share of bills repaid.
    """
    pay = [f"PAY_{i}" for i in (0, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6)]
    bills = [f"BILL_AMT{i}" for i in range(1, 7)]
    paid = [f"PAY_AMT{i}" for i in range(1, 7)]
    return pd.DataFrame(
        {
            "max_delay": frame[pay].clip(lower=0).max(axis=1),
            "months_late": (frame[pay] > 0).sum(axis=1),
            "avg_utilisation": frame[bills].mean(axis=1) / frame["LIMIT_BAL"],
            "pay_ratio": frame[paid].sum(axis=1) / (frame[bills].clip(lower=0).sum(axis=1) + 1),
        },
        index=frame.index,
    )


behaviour = behaviour_summary(X)
design = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "worst delay (per month)": behaviour["max_delay"],
        "average utilisation (per +0.1)": behaviour["avg_utilisation"] * 10,
        "log credit limit (per doubling)": np.log2(X["LIMIT_BAL"]),
        "female (vs male)": (X["SEX"] == 2).astype(int),
        "age (per 10 years)": X["AGE"] / 10,
        "single (vs married)": (X["MARRIAGE"] == 2).astype(int),
        "other marital status (vs married)": (X["MARRIAGE"] == 3).astype(int),
        "university (vs graduate school)": (X["EDUCATION"] == 2).astype(int),
        "high school (vs graduate school)": (X["EDUCATION"] == 3).astype(int),
        "other education (vs graduate school)": (X["EDUCATION"] == 4).astype(int),
    }
)
logit = sm.Logit(y, sm.add_constant(design)).fit(disp=0)
ci = np.exp(logit.conf_int())
odds = pd.DataFrame(
    {"odds_ratio": np.exp(logit.params), "ci_low": ci[0], "ci_high": ci[1], "p": logit.pvalues}
).drop(index="const")
odds.style.format({"odds_ratio": "{:.2f}", "ci_low": "{:.2f}", "ci_high": "{:.2f}", "p": fmt_p})

How to read this.

  • Raw demographic effects are tiny. Every Cramér's V is below 0.08 (education 0.07, sex 0.04, marriage 0.03; age is similar). Even though every chi-square test is "significant" (with 30,000 customers it would be), the effect sizes say demographics barely relate to default. Raw gaps: men default 24.2% vs 20.8% for women; university and high-school graduates default a bit more than graduate-school customers. (The undocumented education codes show strangely low default rates, but they cover only about 1% of customers.)
  • Adjusted odds ratios (all with the other features held fixed):
    • Behaviour dominates. Each extra month of worst delay multiplies the odds of default by about 2.1 (95% CI 2.02 to 2.14), and a doubling of the credit limit multiplies them by about 0.86 (CI 0.84 to 0.88). Average utilisation adds nothing detectable once those are known (OR 1.01, p ≈ 0.11).
    • Demographics are small but not zero. Women have about 9% lower odds than men (OR 0.91, CI 0.86 to 0.97), single customers about 17% lower than married ones (OR 0.83), and each 10 extra years of age raises the odds by about 5% (OR 1.05). University and high-school customers are not distinguishable from graduate-school customers (ORs 1.00 and 0.94, CIs crossing 1). The one odd entry, "other" education (OR 0.36), is the undocumented-code group (about 1% of customers), so we should not read anything into it.
    • These effects are small but not nothing, which is exactly why section 11 asks whether using them would be fair.

8. H4: overlapping bill columns¶

What: the six monthly bill columns record almost the same thing (a customer's balance carries from month to month). The variance inflation factor (VIF) says how much a coefficient's uncertainty is inflated by overlap with the other columns (below 5 is fine, above 10 is serious).

Putting all six into a plain regression gives unstable, hard-to-read coefficients (the same "echo" problem as in the graduate-admission project). That is why we built the four summary features above (worst delay, months late, average utilisation, payment ratio): they compress the overlapping columns into a few meaningful numbers.

9. H5: a leak-free model ladder (and do we need the demographics?)¶

What: the practical question: how well can a model rank customers by default risk, and which ingredients earn their place? A ladder:

  1. Approve everyone: the do-nothing baseline.
  2. Logistic regression on the raw columns, then with the four behaviour summaries added.
  3. Gradient boosting (HistGradientBoostingClassifier), XGBoost (the legacy notebook's model, now with modern settings) and a random forest, all with the summaries.
  4. Ablation: the same boosting model without SEX, AGE and MARRIAGE. H₀: removing them changes nothing.

How we avoid cheating (data leakage). In the legacy script the scaler was fitted on all customers before cross-validation, so the test folds had influenced the scaling. Here every step lives inside a model Pipeline, so it is learned from training customers only. We use stratified folds (each keeps the 22% default rate), repeated 3 times (15 train/test splits) and the Nadeau-Bengio correction for confidence intervals: the 15 scores aren't independent because the splits reuse mostly the same customers, much like several judges who read the same pages of a report, so a plain interval would be too narrow.

How we score. ROC-AUC is the headline (0.5 = a coin flip, 1.0 = perfect ranking). We also report average precision (AP) and the Brier score (the average squared error of the predicted probabilities; lower is better; "approve everyone" scores 0.172).

In [10]:
def add_behaviour(frame: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Appends the plain-English behaviour summaries to the feature table.

    Args:
        frame: Customer feature table.

    Returns:
        Table with the original columns plus the four summaries.
    """
    return pd.concat([frame, behaviour_summary(frame)], axis=1)


X_eng = add_behaviour(X)
PROTECTED = ["SEX", "AGE", "MARRIAGE"]
BOOSTING = {
    "max_depth": 3,
    "learning_rate": 0.05,
    "max_iter": 300,
    "early_stopping": False,
    "random_state": SEED,
}


def build_models() -> dict[str, tuple[object, pd.DataFrame]]:
    """Builds the ladder as (model, feature table) pairs. Scaling lives inside each model.

    Returns:
        Model name mapped to an unfitted estimator and the features it should see.
    """
    return {
        "Approve everyone": (DummyClassifier(strategy="prior"), X),
        "Logistic regression, raw columns": (
            make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression(max_iter=3000)),
            X,
        ),
        "Logistic regression + summaries": (
            make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression(max_iter=3000)),
            X_eng,
        ),
        "Gradient boosting + summaries": (HistGradientBoostingClassifier(**BOOSTING), X_eng),
        "XGBoost + summaries": (
            XGBClassifier(
                n_estimators=300,
                learning_rate=0.05,
                max_depth=3,
                subsample=0.8,
                colsample_bytree=0.7,
                random_state=SEED,
                n_jobs=4,
                eval_metric="logloss",
            ),
            X_eng,
        ),
        "Random forest + summaries": (
            RandomForestClassifier(300, min_samples_leaf=20, random_state=SEED, n_jobs=-1),
            X_eng,
        ),
        "Boosting without SEX, AGE, MARRIAGE": (
            HistGradientBoostingClassifier(**BOOSTING),
            X_eng.drop(columns=PROTECTED),
        ),
    }


def corrected_ci(scores: np.ndarray, n_train: int, n_test: int) -> tuple[float, float, float]:
    """95% CI for a mean CV score using the Nadeau-Bengio variance correction.

    Args:
        scores: Per-split scores.
        n_train: Training rows per split.
        n_test: Test rows per split.

    Returns:
        Mean, CI lower bound, CI upper bound.
    """
    k = len(scores)
    se = np.sqrt((1 / k + n_test / n_train) * np.var(scores, ddof=1))
    half = stats.t.ppf(0.975, k - 1) * se
    return float(scores.mean()), float(scores.mean() - half), float(scores.mean() + half)


def corrected_paired_p(diff: np.ndarray, n_train: int, n_test: int) -> float:
    """Two-sided p-value for "do two models differ?" on identical splits.

    Args:
        diff: Per-split score differences between two models.
        n_train: Training rows per split.
        n_test: Test rows per split.

    Returns:
        p-value from the corrected resampled t-test.
    """
    k = len(diff)
    se = np.sqrt((1 / k + n_test / n_train) * np.var(diff, ddof=1))
    return float(2 * stats.t.sf(abs(diff.mean() / se), k - 1))
In [11]:
cv = RepeatedStratifiedKFold(n_splits=CV_SPLITS, n_repeats=CV_REPEATS, random_state=SEED)
n_test = len(X) // CV_SPLITS
n_train = len(X) - n_test
scoring = {"auc": "roc_auc", "ap": "average_precision", "brier": "neg_brier_score"}

auc_scores, rows = {}, {}
for name, (model, features) in build_models().items():
    res = cross_validate(model, features, y, cv=cv, scoring=scoring)
    auc_scores[name] = res["test_auc"]
    mean, lo, hi = corrected_ci(res["test_auc"], n_train, n_test)
    rows[name] = {
        "ROC-AUC": mean,
        "AUC low": lo,
        "AUC high": hi,
        "AP": res["test_ap"].mean(),
        "Brier": -res["test_brier"].mean(),
    }
results = pd.DataFrame(rows).T
results[["ROC-AUC", "AP", "Brier"]].round(4)

How to read this. (ROC-AUC and AP: higher is better; Brier: lower is better.)

  • Approve everyone: AUC 0.50, AP 0.22 (the default rate), Brier 0.172.
  • Plain logistic regression on the raw columns: AUC ≈ 0.72. Adding the four behaviour summaries lifts it to ≈ 0.76: how the repayment codes are summarised mattered more than which model we used, because the raw codes mix "paid in full" with "months late".
  • Boosting, XGBoost and the random forest all land at AUC ≈ 0.785 (AP ≈ 0.56, Brier ≈ 0.133): a clear step up from logistic regression, but nearly identical to each other, which suggests a ceiling set by the information in the data, not by the algorithm.
  • Dropping SEX, AGE and MARRIAGE costs almost nothing: AUC ≈ 0.785 either way (0.7847 vs 0.7856).

The paired tests tell us which of those gaps are real.

  • XGBoost and the random forest are indistinguishable from boosting (differences within ±0.002, paired p ≈ 0.11 and 0.26): we fail to reject H₀. Three different tree ensembles hit the same ceiling.

10. H6: can we trust the probabilities?¶

What: a bank doesn't just rank customers: it prices risk, sets limits and reserves capital using the predicted probability itself. So we check calibration: among customers the model scores at "20% default risk", do about 20% really default? We use cross_val_predict to get an honest probability for every customer from a model that never saw them. The calibration (reliability) curve plots predicted risk against actual default rate in ten risk bands; the diagonal is perfect. The Hosmer-Lemeshow test asks H₀: the predicted and observed default counts agree in every band.

In [14]:
final_features = X_eng.drop(columns=PROTECTED)
final_model = HistGradientBoostingClassifier(**BOOSTING)
proba = cross_val_predict(
    final_model,
    final_features,
    y,
    cv=StratifiedKFold(CV_SPLITS, shuffle=True, random_state=SEED),
    method="predict_proba",
)[:, 1]
proba = pd.Series(proba, index=y.index)

bands = pd.qcut(proba, 10, duplicates="drop")
calibration = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "predicted": proba.groupby(bands, observed=True).mean(),
        "observed": y.groupby(bands, observed=True).mean(),
        "customers": y.groupby(bands, observed=True).size(),
    }
)
expected = calibration["predicted"] * calibration["customers"]
observed = calibration["observed"] * calibration["customers"]
hl_stat = (((observed - expected) ** 2) / (expected * (1 - calibration["predicted"]))).sum()
hl_p = stats.chi2.sf(hl_stat, len(calibration) - 2)
brier = float(((proba - y) ** 2).mean())
brier_baseline = float(((y.mean() - y) ** 2).mean())
print(
    f"Brier score {brier:.4f} vs {brier_baseline:.4f} for the base rate "
    f"(skill {1 - brier / brier_baseline:.1%})"
)
print(f"Hosmer-Lemeshow: chi2({len(calibration) - 2}) = {hl_stat:.1f}, p = {hl_p:.2f}")
calibration.round(3).T

How to read this. The curve hugs the diagonal across the whole range: customers the model scores at about 5% default roughly 5%, those at about 70% default at roughly that rate. The Brier skill of about 22% says the probabilities are meaningfully better than just quoting the 22% base rate to everyone. The Hosmer-Lemeshow test gives χ²(8) ≈ 24 and p ≈ 0.003, so formally we reject H₀: the probabilities are not perfectly calibrated. But read the table and the size of the gaps: the biggest differences between predicted and observed rates are about 2 percentage points (for example 20.1% predicted against 18.3% observed in the seventh band), and most are within 1 point. With about 3,000 customers per band, the test is sensitive enough to detect gaps that small, so "statistically detectable" is not the same as "practically important". Gradient boosting's probabilities are close enough to use as probabilities, with a slight tendency to over-state risk in the middle bands, not only as a ranking.

The histogram shows why the model is useful: most customers get a low predicted risk, with a long tail of high-risk ones where the decisions matter.

11. H7: deciding who to decline, and is it fair?¶

The decision rule¶

What: to turn a probability into a decision we need the costs. We assume (clearly labelled, and you can change the constants at the top of the notebook) that approving a customer who then defaults costs 5 units, and declining a customer who would have paid costs 1 unit of lost profit. When probabilities are calibrated, decision theory gives the best rule directly: decline when p ≥ 1 / (1 + 5) ≈ 0.167. We confirm this by scanning every threshold on the out-of-fold probabilities.

In [16]:
is_default = y.to_numpy() == 1
p_values = proba.to_numpy()


def decision_cost(threshold: float) -> float:
    """Total cost of declining everyone whose predicted risk is at or above ``threshold``.

    Args:
        threshold: Probability cut-off.

    Returns:
        Missed-default cost plus lost-customer cost, in the assumed units.
    """
    decline = p_values >= threshold
    missed = (is_default & ~decline).sum()
    lost = (~is_default & decline).sum()
    return float(COST_MISSED_DEFAULT * missed + COST_LOST_CUSTOMER * lost)


theory_threshold = COST_LOST_CUSTOMER / (COST_LOST_CUSTOMER + COST_MISSED_DEFAULT)
grid = np.linspace(0.01, 0.99, 197)
costs = np.array([decision_cost(t) for t in grid])
empirical_threshold = float(grid[costs.argmin()])
approve_all_cost = COST_MISSED_DEFAULT * is_default.sum()
decline_all_cost = COST_LOST_CUSTOMER * (~is_default).sum()

print(
    f"Theory-optimal threshold: {theory_threshold:.3f}; empirical optimum on out-of-fold "
    f"probabilities: {empirical_threshold:.3f}"
)
print(
    f"Cost at the theory threshold: {decision_cost(theory_threshold):,.0f} units  |  "
    f"approve everyone: {approve_all_cost:,.0f}  |  decline everyone: {decline_all_cost:,.0f}"
)
print(
    f"Saving versus approving everyone: "
    f"{1 - decision_cost(theory_threshold) / approve_all_cost:.0%}"
)

Theory-optimal threshold: 0.167; empirical optimum on out-of-fold probabilities: 0.155
Cost at the theory threshold: 16,471 units  |  approve everyone: 33,150  |  decline everyone: 23,335
Saving versus approving everyone: 50%

How to read this. The empirical best threshold on the out-of-fold data (0.155) is very close to the theoretical 0.167, a nice confirmation that the probabilities are close to calibrated: decision theory only works when they are. Declining everyone whose predicted risk is above 0.167 costs about 16,500 units against 33,150 for approving everyone (a saving of 50%) and 23,335 for declining everyone (29% cheaper).

What that rule means in practice: because a missed default is assumed to cost five times as much as a lost good customer, the rule is aggressive: it declines about 43% of all customers and wrongly declines about one in three good customers (see the FPR column below) in order to catch about three in four defaulters. That is the honest consequence of the 5:1 assumption, not a flaw in the model. The cost ratio of 5:1 is an assumption; a different ratio moves the threshold, but the method stays the same.

Fairness audit¶

What: a model that uses no demographic columns can still treat groups differently, through features that correlate with them. So we audit the decisions at the threshold above, using the honest out-of-fold probabilities. For each group we report:

  • the decline rate (how often customers in the group are declined),
  • the false-positive rate (FPR): of customers who would have repaid, the share we wrongly declined (the harm to a good customer), and
  • the true-positive rate (TPR): of customers who did default, the share we correctly flagged.

H₀: the FPR is the same for the two groups (tested between men and women with a two-proportion z-test). A fair model, by the "equalised odds" idea, has similar FPR and TPR across groups.

In [17]:
decline = p_values >= theory_threshold
audit_rows = {}
group_defs = {
    "Sex: male": data["SEX"] == 1,
    "Sex: female": data["SEX"] == 2,
    "Age: under 30": data["AGE"] < 30,
    "Age: 30 to 49": data["AGE"].between(30, 49),
    "Age: 50+": data["AGE"] >= 50,
    "Education: graduate": data["EDUCATION"] == 1,
    "Education: university": data["EDUCATION"] == 2,
    "Education: high school": data["EDUCATION"] == 3,
}
for label, mask in group_defs.items():
    m = mask.to_numpy()
    repaid, defaulted = m & ~is_default, m & is_default
    audit_rows[label] = {
        "customers": int(m.sum()),
        "decline rate": decline[m].mean(),
        "FPR (good customers wrongly declined)": decline[repaid].mean(),
        "TPR (defaults caught)": decline[defaulted].mean(),
    }
audit = pd.DataFrame(audit_rows).T


def two_proportion_p(group_a: str, group_b: str, column: str) -> tuple[float, float]:
    """z-test for a difference in a rate between two groups of the audit table.

    Args:
        group_a: First group label (a key of ``group_defs``).
        group_b: Second group label.
        column: ``"FPR"`` or ``"TPR"``.

    Returns:
        Difference in rates (a minus b) and the two-sided p-value.
    """
    counts, sizes = [], []
    for label in (group_a, group_b):
        m = group_defs[label].to_numpy()
        base = (m & ~is_default) if column == "FPR" else (m & is_default)
        counts.append(int(decline[base].sum()))
        sizes.append(int(base.sum()))
    p = proportions_ztest(counts, sizes)[1]
    return counts[0] / sizes[0] - counts[1] / sizes[1], float(p)


fpr_diff, fpr_p = two_proportion_p("Sex: female", "Sex: male", "FPR")
tpr_diff, tpr_p = two_proportion_p("Sex: female", "Sex: male", "TPR")
print(
    f"Female minus male FPR: {fpr_diff:+.3f} (p = {fpr_p:.3f});  TPR: {tpr_diff:+.3f} "
    f"(p = {tpr_p:.3f})"
)
audit.style.format(
    {
        "decline rate": "{:.1%}",
        "FPR (good customers wrongly declined)": "{:.1%}",
        "TPR (defaults caught)": "{:.1%}",
    }
)

    fontsize=11,
)
fig.tight_layout()
fig.savefig(OUT_DIR / "07_fairness_audit.png", dpi=150)
plt.show()

How to read this.

  • Sex: the model never saw the SEX column, yet its decisions differ by sex. Women are declined less often (41.2% against 45.5% for men) and, among customers who would have repaid, women are wrongly declined 3.4 percentage points less often (FPR 32.7% against 36.0%; two-proportion z-test p < 0.001, so we reject H₀). The share of real defaulters caught is similar (TPR 73.5% against 75.2%, p ≈ 0.12, not significant). This matches the raw data, where men default somewhat more (24.2% against 20.8%), but it means the two groups do not have identical error rates.
  • Age: customers under 30 (FPR 37.8%) and over 50 (36.8%) are wrongly declined more often than those aged 30 to 49 (31.6%). Their true-positive rates (77.3%, 74.0%, 72.5%) move the same way.
  • Education: the false-positive rate climbs from 30.9% for graduate-school customers to 35.6% for university and 39.4% for high-school customers, a spread of about 8.5 points, and the true-positive rate climbs with it (72.8%, 74.5%, 77.1%).
  • Reading the pattern: groups with a higher real default rate are declined more often and also suffer more false declines, which is what you would expect from a threshold applied to everyone. Whether a gap of 3 to 9 points in wrongful declines is acceptable is a policy and legal question, not a statistical one. What the statistics can do is measure it, which is what this audit does.
  • Why this audit matters. Leaving demographic columns out is not the same as being fair: other features (the credit limit, repayment history) can carry the same information indirectly, as we see here. We have only checked three characteristics at one threshold, with no causal analysis of why rates differ and no intersections (such as young women). A real credit-scoring system in most countries is regulated and would need a far more thorough review.
  • Why this audit matters. Leaving demographic columns out is not the same as being fair: other features (the credit limit, utilisation) can carry the same information indirectly. We have only checked three protected characteristics at one threshold, with no causal analysis of why rates differ. A real credit-scoring system in most countries is regulated, and would need a far more thorough review.

12. 🎯 Takeaways¶

  1. Recent payment behaviour is the strongest clue. Default rates run from about 13% (paid on time) to about 34% (one month late) to about 69% (two months late); Cramér's V ≈ 0.42 (large).
  2. A smaller credit limit goes with higher default (median 90,000 vs 150,000; Cliff's δ ≈ −0.24), probably partly because banks give safer-looking customers bigger limits.
  3. Demographics barely matter (Cramér's V below 0.08), and removing SEX, AGE and MARRIAGE costs nothing detectable (ΔAUC −0.0008, paired p ≈ 0.13), so the fairer model is also free.
  4. How you summarise repayment history matters more than the algorithm. Logistic regression rises from AUC 0.72 to 0.76 with four behaviour summaries, and three different tree models tie at 0.785.
  5. The probabilities are usable, not perfect. Brier skill is about 22%, and although the Hosmer-Lemeshow test formally rejects perfect calibration (p ≈ 0.003), the gaps are at most about 2 points. A cost-based threshold of about 0.167 (empirical optimum 0.155) cuts the cost by 50% versus approving everyone, at the price of wrongly declining about one in three good customers.
  6. "No demographic columns" is not a fairness guarantee. Auditing the decisions shows women wrongly declined 3.4 points less often than men (p < 0.001), and the false-decline rate climbing from 31% to 39% from graduate-school to high-school customers.

13. ⚠️ Limitations and edge cases¶

  • One bank, one country, 2005. Taiwanese cardholders during a period of heavy card debt; the patterns may not transfer to other banks, countries or the present day.
  • Only about 6 months of history. Defaults after longer periods are not captured.
  • "Default" is one month ahead. A customer who defaults two months later counts as a non-default here.
  • Cost ratio is an assumption. The 5:1 ratio is illustrative; real costs depend on the loan amount, interest and recovery.
  • Selection bias. We only see customers the bank already approved, so we can't say anything about applicants who were declined.
  • Fairness audit is limited. Three characteristics, one threshold, no causal analysis, and no checks on intersections (such as young women).
  • Undocumented codes. EDUCATION 0, 5, 6 and MARRIAGE 0 were folded into "other" (about 1.3% of customers), which hides whatever they really mean.
  • Association, not cause. Nothing here says that paying late causes default, only that it predicts it.
  • Modest tuning. The tree models use sensible fixed settings without a full hyper-parameter search; the legacy script's RandomizedSearchCV ran only one random trial (n_iter=1), which is not a search at all.
